details:
**The School of Athens**
Raphael's most famous fresco (c. 1509–1511), depicting the great thinkers of antiquity gathered beneath a grand barrel-vaulted classical arch. At the center, Plato (modeled on Leonardo da Vinci, holding the Timaeus) points upward toward the realm of Forms, while Aristotle (holding the Nicomachean Ethics) gestures forward and down toward the earth. Statues of Apollo and Athena (Minerva) stand in niches in the background.

**Figures in The School of Athens**
Euclid bends to draw a circle with a compass as students watch, Pythagoras writes in a book, and Diogenes of Sinope sprawls on the steps in a blue robe. A brooding Heraclitus, leaning on a marble block and writing, was added as a portrait of Michelangelo. At the right edge, Ptolemy and Zoroaster hold a terrestrial and celestial globe next to Raphael's own self-portrait.

**Stanza della Segnatura**
One of four rooms in the Vatican's Apostolic Palace, now called the Raphael Rooms (Stanze di Raffaello), that Pope Julius II commissioned Raphael to decorate. Its four walls depict Philosophy (The School of Athens), Theology (La Disputa), Poetry (The Parnassus), and Law (The Cardinal Virtues, in which Fortitude pets a lion, Temperance holds reins, and two-faced Prudence looks in a mirror).

**La Disputa**
The Disputation of the Holy Sacrament, the fresco facing The School of Athens in the Stanza della Segnatura. It is divided into a heavenly level, with Christ enthroned between Mary and John the Baptist, saints, and prophets on clouds, and an earthly level where theologians debate around an altar holding a monstrance with the Eucharist, symbolizing the doctrine of transubstantiation.

**Madonna of the Goldfinch**
A painting (c. 1505–1506) in which the young John the Baptist hands a goldfinch, a symbol of Christ's Passion, to the infant Jesus as the Virgin Mary looks up from a book. It shattered into about seventeen pieces when its owner's house collapsed in 1547 and was later restored. Raphael painted many other Madonnas, including the Madonna of the Meadow (Madonna del Prato) and La Belle Jardinière.

**Sistine Madonna**
An altarpiece (c. 1512) for the church of San Sisto in Piacenza, now in Dresden, showing the Virgin and Child standing barefoot on clouds between Pope Sixtus II and Saint Barbara. Two bored-looking cherubs leaning their arms on the ledge at the bottom have become one of the most reproduced images in art.

**The Parnassus**
A fresco in the Stanza della Segnatura showing Apollo playing a lira da braccio on Mount Parnassus, surrounded by the nine Muses and famous poets including Homer, Dante, and Sappho. Raphael based the face of the blind Homer on the head of Laocoön from the ancient sculpture Laocoön and His Sons, rediscovered in 1506.

**Perugino and The Marriage of the Virgin**
Raphael trained under Pietro Perugino, whose influence shows in his early works. His Marriage of the Virgin (Lo Sposalizio, 1504) closely resembles Perugino's version, with a domed temple in the background and a rejected suitor breaking his rod over his knee in the foreground. His first documented work was the Baronci Altarpiece, and the Oddi Altarpiece shows St. Thomas receiving Mary's girdle.

**Mond Crucifixion**
An early altarpiece (c. 1502–1503), heavily influenced by Perugino, showing Christ on the cross beneath an "INRI" sign, with two angels catching his blood in chalices, flanked by the sun and moon. It is now in the National Gallery, London.

**The Transfiguration**
Raphael's final painting, left unfinished at his death in 1520 and completed by his workshop. Its upper half shows Christ floating in glory on Mount Tabor, while the lower half shows the apostles failing to heal a possessed boy.

**The Triumph of Galatea**
A fresco (c. 1514) in the Villa Farnesina in Rome, commissioned by banker Agostino Chigi. The sea nymph Galatea in a red cloak rides a seashell chariot pulled by two dolphins, surrounded by Tritons, nereids, and cupids shooting arrows.

**Other Raphael Rooms frescoes**
Raphael and his workshop decorated the other Vatican stanze with The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple (a heavenly horseman tramples a man stealing temple treasure), The Mass at Bolsena, and The Fire in the Borgo, in which Pope Leo IV extinguishes a fire and a man carries his father on his back like Aeneas with Anchises. After his death, his student Giulio Romano led the decoration of the Hall of Constantine.

**Portraits of Popes Julius II and Leo X**
Raphael's Portrait of Pope Julius II shows the aging pope seated pensively against a green background, holding a handkerchief. His Portrait of Leo X with Two Cardinals shows the pope in a red velvet cap holding a magnifying glass beside an illuminated book and a silver bell, flanked by two cardinals in red.

**Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione**
A portrait of Raphael's friend, the author of The Book of the Courtier, dressed in a dark fur-trimmed outfit. Castiglione's term "sprezzatura" (effortless grace) is often applied to Raphael's style, contrasted with Michelangelo's "terribilità."

**Raphael Cartoons and La Fornarina**
Raphael designed full-size drawings ("cartoons") for ten tapestries depicting the lives of Saints Peter and Paul for the Sistine Chapel, including The Miraculous Draught of Fishes; seven survive. La Fornarina depicts his supposed lover, a baker's daughter, holding her bare breast, and she may also be the model for La Donna Velata (The Veiled Woman). The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood founded by William Holman Hunt, John Everett Millais, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti rejected the academic art they believed descended from Raphael.
